x-m-el-res-01.title: Turning 'Using It Too Much' into a Question We Can Investigate
x-m-el-res-01.goal: To turn a vague topic into a question that can be checked with data, sort out what must be decided before collecting data.
x-m-el-res-01.material: A club student chose “Students at our school use their smartphones too much” as an inquiry topic. The teacher said, “As this sentence stands, you can neither make a survey nor interpret the results.”
x-m-el-res-01.thinking.1: Turning vague words into measurable words
x-m-el-res-01.prereq.0: Knowing what averages and percentages are (middle school level)
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything that must be decided first, before collecting data.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.hint.0: Look for the parts of the phrase 'too much' that two people might understand differently.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.hint.1: For each item, think about whether two people making the same survey separately would get different results if it were missing.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.o.a: Who is surveyed: all students, one grade, or one class
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.r.a: You missed that if the group is not decided, we cannot know whom the result is about.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.o.b: How to measure 'a lot': hours per day or number of times turned on
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.r.b: If you do not decide what value to use to measure 'a lot,' different people will investigate different things.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.o.c: The standard for 'too': from how many hours counts as a lot
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.r.c: If you do not set a standard, both 'a lot' and 'a little' are possible from the same data.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.o.d: Settling the conclusion sentence to write in the report before the results come out
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.r.d: If you decide the conclusion in advance, it becomes easy to fit the data to that conclusion. What should be decided are the question and the standard.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.o.e: Deciding in advance what colors and fonts to use for the presentation materials
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.r.e: Decoration has little to do with the validity of the investigation. Focus on what is measured and how.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.explain: Only when the group, the way of measuring, and the standard (and the period) are decided can another person find the answer to the same question in the same way. The conclusion should be written after seeing the data.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s1.acc.0: The standard for 'too' can also be decided after collecting the data. But deciding it in advance prevents changing the standard after seeing the results.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.prompt: Put in everything you chose above and rewrite this topic as one sentence of question that can be investigated. (Make the group, the way of measuring, and the period or standard visible.)
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.hint.0: Check one by one whether the sentence contains 'who,' 'measured by what,' 'during when,' and 'from what value.'
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.hint.1: Turn words that differ from person to person, such as 'a lot,' into numbers.
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are the group, the way of measuring, and the period and standard all in the sentence?
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Could another person read your question and investigate in the same way?
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Have value-judging expressions like 'too' and 'a lot' been turned into numerical standards?
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.model.0: For second-year students at our school, what is the average number of hours of smartphone use on a weekday, and what percent of students use it for 3 hours or more?
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.model.1: Among the students in our class, what is the percentage of students whose average daily use over the last week exceeds 4 hours?
x-m-el-res-01.s.s2.modelNote.1: It narrowed the group to one class but made the standard clear.

x-m-el-res-02.title: Can We Draw a Conclusion from This Inquiry Plan?
x-m-el-res-02.goal: Find the parts of an inquiry plan that weaken its conclusion, and suggest how to fix them so it becomes trustworthy.
x-m-el-res-02.material: A student wanted to find out “whether staying long at night self-study raises grades,” and made the inquiry plan below.
x-m-el-res-02.prereq.0: Knowing what an average is (middle school level)
x-m-el-res-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line that makes the conclusion unreliable. (Line numbers start from 1.)
x-m-el-res-02.s.s1.hint.0: Check each line to see 'compared with what' it draws its conclusion.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether night self-study is the only reason the scores went up, or whether there are other possibilities.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s1.line.0: Inquiry question: Do students who stay for night self-study get higher grades?
x-m-el-res-02.s.s1.line.1: Group: 20 students who take part in night self-study
x-m-el-res-02.s.s1.line.2: Method: Find the difference between this semester's midterm and final exam scores.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s1.line.3: Conclusion plan: If the participating students' scores went up on average, write 'night self-study raises grades.'
x-m-el-res-02.s.s1.explain: Line 2 cannot be compared with students who do not take part, so we cannot know whether the rise in scores also happens to other students. Line 4 jumps straight from the scores going up to calling it the cause. Both weaken the conclusion.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s2.prompt: Pick one part to fix and write how changing it would make the conclusion more trustworthy.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write the number or content of the line you will fix, then continue with the changed plan.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s2.hint.1: Add one sentence on what question your changed plan answers.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is the part you fixed connected to the reason the conclusion is hard to trust?
x-m-el-res-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check whether there is still something in the fixed plan that keeps you from declaring a cause?
x-m-el-res-02.s.s2.model.0: Find the change in scores in the same way for 20 students who do not take part in night self-study, compare, and write that there is a relationship only if the participating students rose more.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s2.model.1: Line 4 has to be changed. The rise in scores might be due to other reasons such as test difficulty or individual study, so write only up to 'grades went up' and do not declare the cause.
x-m-el-res-02.s.s2.modelNote.1: This is a direction of correcting how the conclusion is worded.

x-m-el-res-03.title: How Many Students per Grade Should We Survey?
x-m-el-res-03.goal: Decide on your own how to divide the number of people in a sample among groups of different sizes, and explain why you do it that way.
x-m-el-res-03.material: A school has 120 first-year students, 100 second-year students and 80 third-year students, 300 in all. To find out satisfaction with school meals, you want to survey 30 students in all. It is said to be good to match the number chosen from each grade to the proportion of students in that grade, but you decided that, given the circumstances, being off by up to 1 person from the proportional number is fine.
x-m-el-res-03.prereq.0: Percentage and ratio calculation (middle school level)
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.prompt: If 10 students are surveyed from each grade, what is the chance of any one student in the whole school being chosen?
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each grade, compare 'number chosen ÷ total number in that grade.'
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.hint.1: First compare the first-year and the third-year students.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.o.a: All three grades are the same
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.r.a: You thought that if the number chosen is the same, the chance of being chosen is the same. You need to look at each grade's total number as well.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.o.b: First-year students have the highest chance
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the number chosen and missed the ratio to the grade's total number.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.o.c: Third-year students have the highest chance
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.r.c: This is the thinking of comparing the number chosen against the grade's total number.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.o.d: If the grades have different numbers, it cannot be calculated
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.r.d: Even if the numbers differ, you can compare using 'number chosen ÷ grade total.'
x-m-el-res-03.s.s1.explain: For the third year it is 10 out of 80 (one eighth) and for the first year it is 10 out of 120 (one twelfth), so a third-year student has a greater chance of being chosen. If you divide the numbers equally, the degree to which each grade is represented differs.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different ways to divide so that the number chosen is 30 in all. (The difference from the proportional number is 1 person or less for each grade.)
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.hint.0: First find what proportion of the total each grade's number of students makes up.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.hint.1: Start from the values you get by applying that proportion to 30 people, and then raise or lower one grade by 1 person.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The number is an integer of 0 or more.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The number must be an integer of 0 or more.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.fail.c2: The total of the three grades' numbers is not 30.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The first year fits the proportion standard.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The first-year number differs by 2 or more from the number that fits the student proportion.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.ok.c4: The second year fits the proportion standard.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.fail.c4: The second-year number differs by 2 or more from the number that fits the student proportion.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.ok.c5: The third year fits the proportion standard.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.fail.c5: The third-year number differs by 2 or more from the number that fits the student proportion.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.explain: The ratio of students is 120 : 100 : 80, that is 6 : 5 : 4, so dividing 30 people gives 12 : 10 : 8 as the standard. Divisions that go up or down by 1 person from there are also allowed.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.because.prompt: Compared with choosing 10 from every grade, write in what way dividing according to the number of students gives better results.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.because.hint.0: Think about how much power one person in a grade with fewer students has on the overall result when 10 are chosen from each.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put 'represents the whole' into your own words.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation include the difference in the number of students per grade?
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say which grade's opinions are reflected more strongly in the result when 10 are chosen from each?
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.because.model.0: If 10 are chosen from each, the opinions of the third year, which has fewer students, are reflected more strongly in the overall result, so it can lean to one side. If you match the number of students, this leaning is reduced.
x-m-el-res-03.s.s2.because.model.1: Only if it is proportional to the number of students is the chance of being chosen similar for all students, so you can get a result that represents the whole school.

x-m-el-res-04.title: If You Visit the Library Often, Do Your Scores Go Up?
x-m-el-res-04.goal: Follow how your first judgment should change as more data is given one piece at a time, and do not read a correlation straight away as a cause.
x-m-el-res-04.material: The student council asked 200 students how many times they used the library in the past month and what their latest exam score was, and organized the results.
x-m-el-res-04.thinking.2: Fix the conclusion sentence to fit the data
x-m-el-res-04.prereq.0: Knowing what an average is (middle school level)
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose the appropriate judgment.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think about which part of your earlier judgment this new information shakes.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine what would change if you compared only groups with the same conditions.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.info: The 80 students who used the library 4 or more times a month had an average score of 82, and the other 120 students had an average score of 74.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What is the most appropriate judgment from this information alone?
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.after: A difference in averages tells you only that they 'appear together.' You cannot yet know why.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It can be said that library use raised scores by 8 points
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You read the difference in averages straight away as a cause.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It can only be said that the students who used the library have a higher average score
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is the thinking of telling apart a difference in averages from a cause, and saying only as much as the data show.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Library use and scores have nothing to do with each other
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: The averages differ by 8 points, yet you declared there was no relationship.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Before talking about a cause, we need to know more about how the survey was done
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is the thinking of holding off judgment and looking for more needed information.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Most of the students who used the library answered that they also usually self-study for more than 3 hours a day, and among the students who did not use it, only a few were like that.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: How should the judgment change now?
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.after: If the two groups being compared differed in other ways besides the library, you cannot blame the difference in scores only on the library.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Study time may have affected the difference in scores, so it is hard to call it the effect of the library alone
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This is the thinking of checking whether the two groups compared also differed in other ways.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Study time doesn't matter, so keep the judgment that it is because of the library
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You left your first judgment as it was even after seeing the new information.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It has now been proven that the library has nothing to do with scores
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The new information lets you say that 'there may be another reason,' but it has not proven 'no relationship.'
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: There are few students who used it, so all the data should be thrown away
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Throwing away all the data is an excessive reaction. 80 students is a number worth comparing.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.info: When comparing only students with similar study time, the average for students who used the library was 77 and the average for those who did not was 76.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the appropriate judgment now about the first 8-point difference?
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.after: Adjusting the strength of your judgment according to new data is what inquiry is. Having your first judgment turn out wrong is nothing to be ashamed of.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It seems that much of the first 8-point difference overlapped with the difference in study time
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is the thinking of revising the first judgment with the result of a condition-matched comparison.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The first 8-point difference was right and this comparison is wrong
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A comparison that matched study time is fairer, yet you stuck to the first result.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The effect of the library may not be large, but we cannot fix it at 0 from this survey alone
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is the thinking of acknowledging a small difference but avoiding a final claim.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 77 is higher than 76, so the effect of the library is certain
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: A difference of 1 point is small, so it is hard to say the effect is certain from this data alone.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s1.reflect: At first it was easy to read it as 'raised it by 8 points,' but once you learn that study time overlaps, you come to read the same data differently. Recall which information changed your judgment.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s2.prompt: Rewrite the first report sentence 'Library use raises grades by 8 points' to fit this data.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s2.hint.0: If you put the average score numbers in the sentence, it becomes easier for readers to judge.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s2.hint.1: See whether you can write what the data actually showed in place of 'raises.'
x-m-el-res-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your sentence tell apart 'appeared together' from 'is the cause'?
x-m-el-res-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is the result of the comparison that matched study time reflected in the sentence?
x-m-el-res-04.s.s2.model.0: The students who used the library often had an average score 8 points higher, but among students with similar study time the difference was 1 point, so it is hard to declare that library use raised grades.
x-m-el-res-04.s.s2.model.1: A large part of the score difference may be because of long study time (77 versus 76), and the effect of library use cannot be known from this survey alone.

x-m-el-res-05.title: It Worked 40 Times, So Can It Still Be Wrong?
x-m-el-res-05.goal: Find a counterexample yourself to see that even a rule you checked many times can be broken by a single counterexample, and explain the difference between checking and proving.
x-m-el-res-05.material: You put n = 1, 2, 3, …, 10 into the value of n² − n + 41 (n squared minus n plus 41) and got 41, 43, 47, 53, 61, 71, 83, 97, 113, 131, and all of them were prime numbers. A student claims, “For every natural number n, n² − n + 41 is a prime number.”
x-m-el-res-05.prereq.0: The meaning of a prime number (a natural number of 2 or more whose only divisors are 1 and itself)
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.prompt: From the results of checking n = 1 through 10, what is the most appropriate sentence you can say?
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.hint.0: Tell apart whether a sentence speaks about 'the range you checked' or 'all cases.'
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether there are values of n left that you have not checked.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.o.a: All ten were right, so we can consider it to hold for every n
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.r.a: You thought that checking a large number of cases is the same as checking all cases.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.o.b: All ten are prime, so there is almost no chance of a counterexample
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.r.b: You changed it to 'chance,' but infinitely many values of n remain unchecked.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.o.c: Until a non-prime value comes out, we can say this formula is right
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.r.c: Having no counterexample yet is different from always holding.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.o.d: Only n=1 to 10 was checked, and larger n has not been checked yet
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.r.d: This is the thinking of separating the range you checked from the range you did not.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s1.explain: You can say it holds only in the range you checked (n=1 to 10). The other n have not been checked, so 'all n' is still unknown.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different natural numbers n for which n²−n+41 is not a prime number.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what n(n−1) has to be like for the value to be a multiple of 41.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.fail.c1: n must be a natural number of 1 or more.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.ok.c2: n²−n+41 is not a prime number.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.fail.c2: n²−n+41 is a prime number. It cannot be a counterexample.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.explain: If n = 41, then 41² − 41 + 41 = 41² = 1681, which is not a prime number. If n = 42, then 1763 = 41 × 43. Even though many earlier cases were right, a single counterexample breaks 'all n.'
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why the fact that n = 1 through 40 were all prime does not show that 'it is prime for every n.'
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Think about how many examples are needed to break the word 'every.'
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare the number of n you checked with the number of all natural numbers.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation state the difference between 'what was checked' and 'what was proved'?
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you mention the power of a single counterexample?
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.because.model.0: Even one counterexample makes the claim 'for all n' wrong, so having checked 40 cases does not let us say it also holds for later n.
x-m-el-res-05.s.s2.because.model.1: There are endlessly many natural numbers and only some of them were checked, so it may not hold for the n that were not checked.

x-m-el-res-06.title: The Solution Lost a Root When We Divided
x-m-el-res-06.goal: Find the step in an equation solution where a root is lost, explain why, and solve it correctly.
x-m-el-res-06.material: A student solved the equation x² = x (x squared equals x) as follows.
x-m-el-res-06.prereq.0: Being able to handle quadratic equations about the level of x²=x (middle school level)
x-m-el-res-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line that makes the solution untrustworthy. (Line numbers start from 1.)
x-m-el-res-06.s.s1.hint.0: Think about what value an expression cannot take when you divide both sides by it.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s1.hint.1: Tell apart whether line 3 shows only that '1 is a solution' or also that 'only 1 is a solution.'
x-m-el-res-06.s.s1.line.1: Divide both sides by x and get x = 1.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s1.line.2: Substituting x = 1 gives 1 = 1, so it holds.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s1.line.3: So the only solution is x = 1.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s1.explain: In line 2, to divide both sides by the same expression, that expression must not be 0. Because the division was done without checking this, the conclusion 'only one' in line 4 cannot be trusted either. Line 3 is correct, but it does not show that there are no other solutions.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s2.prompt: Explain why this solution is a problem, and write all the correct solutions.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s2.hint.0: Try values of x to find which makes the division in line 2 impossible.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s2.hint.1: Try moving everything over to x²−x=0 and solving without dividing.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your explanation state 'the condition needed when dividing'?
x-m-el-res-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you check by substituting the solutions of your fixed solution into the original equation?
x-m-el-res-06.s.s2.model.0: If x is 0, it is like dividing by 0, which is not allowed. Since x²−x=0, x(x−1)=0, x=0 or x=1.
x-m-el-res-06.s.s2.model.1: Before dividing, you have to look at the case x=0 separately. x=0 satisfies the equation, so the solutions are the two values 0 and 1.

x-m-el-res-07.title: What Should We Do with the 1-Point Response?
x-m-el-res-07.goal: Sort out which ways of handling data are honest and which manipulate the results when the data differ from your expectations, and write it as a report sentence.
x-m-el-res-07.material: To show that “satisfaction with our school's meals is 7 points or higher,” a student asked 10 people to give a score from 1 (very dissatisfied) to 10 (very satisfied). The responses were 7, 8, 6, 7, 8, 7, 9, 6, 1, 7 points, and the average was 6.6 points. The friend who gave 1 point seems to have written it as a joke, but this is not certain. The average of the 9 responses without the 1 is about 7.2 points.
x-m-el-res-07.thinking.0: Evaluate ways of handling the data
x-m-el-res-07.thinking.1: Write a sentence that reports transparently
x-m-el-res-07.prereq.0: Knowing what an average is (middle school level)
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the ways of handling it that can be seen as honest reporting.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether someone who reads each way later could check the process just as it was.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.hint.1: See whether the way of handling was decided after seeing the results.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.o.a: Quietly delete the suspicious 1-point response and report only the average of about 7.2 points
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.r.a: If you quietly delete data on suspicion alone, the reader cannot check the process and cannot tell whether the result was manufactured.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.o.b: Use the average of 6.6 points with all ten included and also write down the 1-point response
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.r.b: This is the thinking of showing the data just as it is without changing it.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.o.c: Change the 1-point response to 6 points so that the average becomes 7 or more, and report that
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.r.c: Changing a value is making up data. You cannot change a number just because it differs from what you expected.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.o.d: Leave out the 1-point response, state the reason, and also write the average with it included, 6.6 points
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.r.d: This is the thinking of letting the reader check the handling process and its effect.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.o.e: Keep adding respondents until the average goes over 7, and stop when it does
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.r.e: If you set it to stop when you like the result, you end up picking a moment when the value happened to come out high.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.explain: Deleting or changing data, or deciding when to stop to fit the result, is manipulation. You may deal with a strange-looking value, but you must state openly how you handled it and show its effect too.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s1.acc.0: Reporting the data just as it is is honest. It is even better if you also know the way of handling the 1-point response separately (d).
x-m-el-res-07.s.s2.prompt: Write, in one or two sentences, an honest average result sentence for the report.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s2.hint.0: The sentence must contain both the average number and how the 1-point response was handled.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether a reader could tell how the result came out from this sentence alone.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Can the reader tell that there was a 1-point response?
x-m-el-res-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Is your choice steering the result in the direction you want?
x-m-el-res-07.s.s2.model.0: The average of the 10 responses is 6.6 points, and if the one 1-point response is excluded it is about 7.2 points.
x-m-el-res-07.s.s2.model.1: There was one 1-point response, and although it looks suspicious I did not delete it; the average with it included is 6.6 points.

x-m-el-res-08.title: Checking the Procedure in a Report Draft
x-m-el-res-08.goal: Find mistakes in citing sources and choosing data in an inquiry report draft, and choose the right way to handle results that differ from expectations.
x-m-el-res-08.material: A student writing a draft inquiry report on sleep time handled the data as follows.
x-m-el-res-08.prereq.0: Some experience of doing a survey
x-m-el-res-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line that has a problem in the inquiry procedure. (Line numbers start from 1.)
x-m-el-res-08.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether a reader can check the data's source and conditions from this line alone.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s1.hint.1: See whether the standard for choosing data was decided before seeing the results.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s1.line.0: Copied a table of teenage sleep time found on the internet as it is, and did not write the source because it is data anyone can see.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s1.line.1: For our class survey, wrote the survey date, number of people, and the question sentence in the report.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s1.line.2: Because the results differed from the hypothesis, chose only the responses of the two classes that fit the hypothesis and analyzed those.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s1.line.3: For data from another school, wrote the organization and year, and also stated that the survey method differs from ours.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s1.explain: Line 1 does not say who made the data, so the reader cannot check it, and it is as if someone else's data were used as one's own. Line 3 made the result by choosing only data that fit the hypothesis. Lines 2 and 4 state the conditions, so the reader can judge.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.prompt: You analyzed the responses of all classes and the hypothesis was not supported. What is the most appropriate way to handle it?
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.hint.0: Check whether each choice shows the reader the first result as it is.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.hint.1: Recall that a result that does not support the hypothesis is also information.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.o.a: The hypothesis can't be wrong, so write that the survey questions were bad and remove the result
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.r.a: You threw out the result because you did not like it.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.o.b: Use all the results as they are, state that the hypothesis was not supported, and look into the reasons
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.r.b: This is the thinking of accepting a result that differs from expectations as a piece of information too.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.o.c: Keep only the classes that fit the hypothesis and remove the other classes' responses from the report
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.r.c: The standard for choosing data has become the result.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.o.d: Put the results that differ from the hypothesis very small at the end of the table, and explain only the parts that fit the hypothesis
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.r.d: You did not hide the result, but you placed it so that the reader would miss it.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.o.e: First report all the results, then survey again with the same question and include both results
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.r.e: This is the thinking of keeping the first result and doing further checks.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.explain: Inquiry means reporting results just as they are even if they differ from the hypothesis, and looking into possible reasons. You can survey again, but you must show the first result too.
x-m-el-res-08.s.s2.acc.0: It is an honest method if you include the first result without hiding it, alongside the result of the new survey.

x-m-el-res-09.title: What the Data Say and What They Do Not
x-m-el-res-09.topic: Stating the limits of a conclusion
x-m-el-res-09.goal: Tell apart sentences that can be read straight from the data from overgeneralizations, and write a conclusion sentence that states its limits.
x-m-el-res-09.material: Right after the last day of exams, 30 students in our class wrote down by themselves their average sleep time per day. Of the 30, 24 (80%) answered that they sleep less than 7 hours. No survey was done of other classes or other days.
x-m-el-res-09.thinking.0: Pick out claims supported by the evidence
x-m-el-res-09.thinking.1: Write a conclusion that includes its limits
x-m-el-res-09.prereq.0: Ratio and percentage calculation (middle school level)
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the sentences supported by this data.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.hint.0: Compare each sentence with the data to see 'about whom' and 'about when' it speaks.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.hint.1: Check that the sentence does not include information that is not in the data (grades, other classes).
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.o.a: About 80% of the students at our school are short on sleep
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.r.a: You extended the result of one class to the whole school.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.o.b: Of the 30 students in our class, 24 answered that they sleep less than 7 hours
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.r.b: This is the thinking of saying only the range the data directly shows.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.o.c: The shorter a student's sleep time, the lower the grades
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.r.c: There is no data on grades, yet you spoke about the relationship between the two.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.o.d: Because it was right after the exams, it is hard to declare it to be their usual sleep time
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.r.d: This is the thinking of doubting the effect the timing of the survey might have on the results.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.o.e: Most high school students in Korea cannot even sleep 7 hours a day
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.r.e: You extended the result of one class to the whole country.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.explain: What the data directly show is b, and d is the limit that, because of the timing of the survey, it is hard to accept it as usual sleep. The rest are sentences that extend beyond the range of the data.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s1.acc.0: This is a sentence that can be read straight from the data. It is even better if you also choose the limit about the timing of the survey (d).
x-m-el-res-09.s.s2.prompt: Write a conclusion from this data in one or two sentences, and state at least two limits along with it.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s2.hint.0: First write in one sentence what the data directly show.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s2.hint.1: Then look for limits from three viewpoints: 'who,' 'when,' and 'how they were asked.'
x-m-el-res-09.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Does your conclusion sentence stay within the range the data directly show?
x-m-el-res-09.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Are there at least two limits, and are they of different kinds?
x-m-el-res-09.s.s2.selfAssess.2: In writing the limits, did you end up erasing the conclusion itself?
x-m-el-res-09.s.s2.model.0: Of the 30 students in our class, 24 answered that they sleep less than 7 hours. However, only one class was surveyed and it was right after exams, so it is hard to generalize to the whole school or to usual sleep time.
x-m-el-res-09.s.s2.model.1: 80% of the 30 respondents said they sleep less than 7 hours, but the answers were self-reported and given right after the exam period, so we cannot say it is accurate, and we cannot know whether other classes are the same.

x-m-el-res-10.title: How Much Can We Trust 70% of 10 People?
x-m-el-res-10.topic: Stating the limits of a conclusion
x-m-el-res-10.goal: Check by making values yourself that a difference found in a small sample can be reversed if only a few people's answers change, and write the conclusion in a suitably weakened form.
x-m-el-res-10.material: A survey of all 400 students in the school found that 260 (65%) were in favor of 'a longer lunch break.' Class A has 20 students, but only the 10 who responded first were surveyed, and 7 (70%) were in favor. A student wrote, “Class A's approval rate is higher than the whole school's.”
x-m-el-res-10.thinking.1: Find cases where the conclusion reverses
x-m-el-res-10.thinking.2: Adjust the strength of a conclusion
x-m-el-res-10.prereq.0: Percentage calculation and inequality judgment (middle school level)
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything else you need to know to judge whether this sentence can be trusted.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.hint.0: Think about whether, for this comparison to be trustworthy, the values must be 'obtained with the same question in the same way.'
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine how the result could change if there are responses you do not yet know.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.o.a: How the 10 respondents were chosen from Class A
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.r.a: How the respondents were chosen is directly tied to whether the result represents the whole class.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.o.b: What the average height of Class A's respondents is
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.r.b: You chose information that has little to do with the approval rate.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.o.c: How many students in Class A have not yet responded
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.r.c: This is the thinking of examining whether the missing responses could change the result.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.r.d: This calculation is already right. What you do not know is not the calculation but the nature of the data.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.o.e: Whether the question sentences asking about approval were the same in the two surveys
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.r.e: This is the thinking of checking whether the two values being compared were obtained on the same basis.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s1.explain: Depending on how respondents were chosen, how many did not respond, and whether the question sentences were the same, the comparison of 70% versus 65% can change. Height and a calculation that is already right are not needed for the judgment.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.prompt: If x of the other 10 students in Class A approve, then the number of approvals in the whole of Class A (20 students) is 7+x. Find 3 different values of x for which this approval rate is 65% or less of the whole school's.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.hint.0: First find the number of approvals in the whole of Class A at which the rate is 65% or less.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.hint.1: Subtract the 7 who already approved from that number to set the range of x.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer from 0 to 10.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of the others must be an integer from 0 to 10.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.ok.c2: The approval rate for all of Class A is 65% or less.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The approval rate for all of Class A is higher than 65%.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.explain: The approval rate for Class A's 20 students is (7+x)÷20. If x is 6 or less, it is 65% or less, and the sentence 'higher than the school' is reversed. The conclusion can change depending on the answers of the other 10.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.because.prompt: Write how the sentence 'Class A's approval rate is higher than the whole school's' should be rewritten based on this result.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.because.hint.0: Think about how much power the other 10 have on the result when only 10 responses exist.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check whether your rewritten sentence includes 'why we cannot declare it.'
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does your sentence stay within the range of the data you have now?
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Does it include that the result could change depending on the remaining responses?
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.because.model.0: Only 10 people responded, so the result could change depending on the answers of the other 10, which makes it hard to declare that Class A is higher.
x-m-el-res-10.s.s2.because.model.1: With a small sample, the conclusion can reverse. 70% versus 65% can switch order if only a few responses differ, so we cannot confirm that Class A is higher.
